lessons.title: Run Python in your own workspace
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 1 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Run a saved script using a known interpreter.
Create a project environment.
Explain why no extra packages are needed.

exercises.title: The package went to another interpreter
exercises.prompt: Your editor runs .venv/bin/python, but a bare pip command installed a package elsewhere. Which command targets the intended interpreter?
options: Copy the whole system Python folder
hints: Compare the interpreter paths.
pip can belong to a different installation.
Run pip as a module of the intended Python.
exercises.solution: Use .venv/bin/python -m pip so installation belongs to the Python running your project. Changing the filename or copying system files does not fix the interpreter mismatch.

exercises.title: Running the saved source
exercises.prompt: You edited welcome.py but the terminal still shows yesterday’s message. What should you check first?
options: Save the file and confirm the path of the script being run
hints: The interpreter runs a file from disk.
The editor may hold unsaved changes.
Check both the saved contents and command path.
exercises.solution: Save the edited file and check which file the command names. The interpreter does not run unsaved editor text; extra packages cannot change that.

lessons.title: Values, conversion & exact amounts
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 2 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Distinguish text, numbers and missing values.
Represent project amounts as integer cents.
Format cents without floating-point conversion.

exercises.title: The invoice total is text
exercises.prompt: What is the result of `subtotal = "40"; tax = "5"; total = subtotal + tax`?
hints: Both inputs are strings.
The + operator can join text.
There is no numeric conversion here.
exercises.solution: The result is the string "405". Convert or parse the values under the amount contract before adding them. Python does not infer numeric intent from these strings.

exercises.title: A zero budget is intentional
exercises.prompt: A budget of zero must disable spending; None means use the default 500. Which expression preserves that rule?
options: 500 if budget is None else budget
hints: Zero and missing are different states.
or treats zero as false.
Check the missing marker explicitly.
exercises.solution: Use an explicit None check. That substitutes 500 only for missing input, while a deliberate zero remains zero.

lessons.title: Text, lists & dictionaries
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 3 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Choose collections for expenses and categories.
Normalize text without losing valid content.
Recognize shared mutable objects.

exercises.title: Cleaning keeps the old string
exercises.prompt: After `label = " Food "; cleaned = label.strip().lower()`, what are label and cleaned?
hints: Strings are not changed in place.
Each method returns text.
The result is assigned to a different name.
exercises.solution: The original label stays " Food " and cleaned is "food". String methods return new values; they do not edit the original string.

exercises.title: Count purchases, not unique categories
exercises.prompt: Three rows have categories food, food, travel. Which pair preserves all purchases and supports a unique category list?
options: A list of rows and a set of category names
A dictionary with one fixed key
hints: Duplicate purchases are real records.
A set removes duplicate values.
Use different collections for different questions.
exercises.solution: Keep purchases in a list and distinct category names in a set. A set of categories cannot tell you how many food purchases occurred.

lessons.title: Decisions, loops & category totals
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 4 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Read indented branches and loops.
Accumulate totals without resetting earlier work.
Handle empty input deliberately.

exercises.title: The disappearing subtotal
exercises.prompt: A summary loop executes `totals = {}` at the start of every iteration. Why does the report contain only the latest contribution?
options: The loop resets accumulated state for each row
Python always sorts away older rows
hints: Track totals after each iteration.
Look at when a fresh dictionary is created.
The starting state must survive the loop.
exercises.solution: Create totals once before the loop. Resetting it inside throws away the previous rows, even if the addition for the current row is correct.

exercises.title: A valid file with no expenses
exercises.prompt: A CSV has the required header and no data records. Under the project contract, what should the summary be?
options: Zero rows, zero total, and an empty category mapping
hints: Header validity and row count are separate.
A for loop may run zero times.
Choose starting values that already represent no expenses.
exercises.solution: The initialized zero count, zero total and empty mapping are the correct report. Header-only input is valid; a file with no header is a different case.

lessons.title: Small functions & amount validation
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 5 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Separate returned values from printed output.
Validate amount text against a clear contract.
Keep per-call state separate.

exercises.title: It prints but returns nothing
exercises.prompt: A test expects `format_cents(105) == "1.05"`, but the function only calls print with that text. Why does the test fail?
options: print returns None rather than the displayed text
Every function automatically returns its last expression
hints: Screen output and returned values are separate.
Check the value given back to the caller.
Use return for reusable calculations.
exercises.solution: print displays the text but returns None. The caller needs the string, so return it; the command wrapper can print it later.

exercises.title: More precision than the contract allows
exercises.prompt: The amount parser receives "6.789". The contract allows at most two digits after the dot. What should it do?
hints: The contract chooses rejection, not rounding.
Do not silently change submitted amounts.
A clear error preserves the distinction from valid input.
exercises.solution: Reject the amount with ValueError. Rounding or dropping digits changes data without permission; zero is a valid amount and cannot stand for failure.

lessons.title: Helpful errors & practical debugging
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 6 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Read a traceback and reproduce a failure.
Catch expected errors without hiding bugs.
Add useful record context to failures.

exercises.title: A bug disguised as a free expense
exercises.prompt: A parser has `except Exception: return 0`. What is the main problem?
options: Exceptions cannot be caught in Python
It can hide programming bugs and report invalid input as a valid zero
It makes valid zero amounts negative
hints: Ask which failures are expected.
Zero already has a real meaning.
Catch narrowly and preserve the failure signal.
exercises.solution: This catches unrelated bugs and turns failures into success-looking data. Catch expected input errors specifically and let the caller report them clearly.

exercises.title: Finding an invalid CSV record
exercises.prompt: A conversion failed on logical record 5. Which error best helps the user while retaining diagnostic cause?
options: Raise ValueError("record 5: invalid amount") from the original error
hints: The user needs location and reason.
Developers may still need the original cause.
The project rejects the whole invalid input.
exercises.solution: Include the record and field in the message and chain the original error with from. Empty or partial reports would hide a failed import.

lessons.title: Read CSV & produce JSON safely
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 7 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Read UTF-8 files inside a with block.
Validate CSV headers and record shape.
Emit JSON only after the full input succeeds.

exercises.title: A comma inside a category
exercises.prompt: A CSV data record is `"food, snacks",2.50`. Which reader preserves the category as one field?
options: csv.DictReader configured for the CSV format
hints: Quotes give the comma a different meaning.
A raw split does not understand CSV quoting.
Use the parser designed for the format.
exercises.solution: Use the CSV parser. It understands quoted fields, so food, snacks remains one category. eval would execute code and is not a data parser.

exercises.title: Success printed before validation ends
exercises.prompt: Your CLI prints a report after each record, then record 8 is invalid. What change honors the all-or-error output contract?
options: Keep the earlier JSON because some rows worked
Compute and validate the complete summary before printing one JSON document
Print the traceback inside the JSON
hints: stdout is meant to contain one successful report.
A later failure invalidates the whole input.
Separate summary calculation from output.
exercises.solution: Validate the full input before printing JSON. If any record fails, report the error on stderr and exit nonzero without partial success output.

lessons.title: Modules & command-line tools
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 8 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Keep imports free of command execution.
Use argparse and the main guard.
Distinguish stdout, stderr and exit status.

exercises.title: Importing starts the command
exercises.prompt: Importing cli from a unit test immediately parses the test runner’s arguments. What structure prevents that side effect?
options: Run argument parsing in every module
Use a main function called only under the __main__ guard
Wrap all code in except Exception
hints: Imports execute module-level statements.
Definitions can be imported without calling them.
Direct execution needs an explicit entry point.
exercises.solution: Define main and call it under if __name__ == "__main__". A test can then import functions without starting the command.

exercises.title: A script needs reliable failure reporting
exercises.prompt: The CSV is missing. What should the supplied expense CLI emit under its contract?
options: Exit 0 and output an empty report
Print JSON followed by an error
A helpful stderr message, no stdout report, and exit status 2
Only a debug print and exit 0
hints: Machine callers inspect output and status.
Missing input is not a successful empty file.
Keep errors separate from successful JSON.
exercises.solution: The contract uses stderr plus status 2 for expected input/file errors. stdout remains empty so a caller cannot mistake a failure for a valid report.

lessons.title: Test and build your expense tracker
lessons.summary: Python foundations · lesson 9 of 9 · expense-tracker path
objectives: Write success, boundary and failure tests.
Complete the provided CLI project contract.
Present code and evidence for separate review.

exercises.title: A test that never runs your parser
exercises.prompt: A test replaces parse_amount with a mock that returns 250, then checks that it returns 250. What does this prove?
options: The amount format is fully implemented
Only that the mock returns its configured value
hints: Locate which implementation actually runs.
The real parser was replaced.
Test the real function with representative inputs.
exercises.solution: The test exercises the mock, not the amount parser. Call the real parser with valid, boundary and invalid text to check its contract.

exercises.title: The second call inherits yesterday’s totals
exercises.prompt: All single-call summary tests pass, but a global totals dictionary is reused. Which test is most likely to expose it?
options: Call summarize_rows twice with different inputs and check the second result contains only its own rows
Check only that the function exists
Increase the sample file size without checking output
hints: Shared state can outlive one call.
One call may look correct in isolation.
Check independent calls back to back.
exercises.solution: Two sequential calls expose leftover state without timing or threads. Each summary should start with fresh totals unless the contract explicitly promises accumulation.

lessons.title: Text, bytes & Unicode without surprises
lessons.summary: Python in practice · lesson 1 of 5 · event-timeline repair
objectives: Distinguish bytes from decoded text.
Reject bad UTF-8 instead of hiding loss.
Normalize labels under an explicit policy.

exercises.title: Two lengths for the same name
exercises.prompt: For `text = "café"`, what are len(text) and len(text.encode("utf-8"))?
options: Both depend on the terminal font
hints: Text and bytes are different types.
An accented character can take multiple UTF-8 bytes.
Count four code points, then five encoded bytes.
exercises.solution: The text has four code points and the UTF-8 encoding has five bytes. The display width does not change either count. Do not slice encoded data as if one byte always means one character.

exercises.title: A decoded name quietly loses data
exercises.prompt: A UTF-8 input contains invalid bytes. The reporting contract requires preserving labels exactly under its normalization rule. What should decoding do?
options: Reject the invalid encoding with a clear error
Replace every non-ASCII character with a question mark
hints: The contract promises a known encoding.
Ignoring bytes silently changes the input.
A useful failure is better than an invented label.
exercises.solution: Reject invalid UTF-8. Ignoring or replacing bytes can change labels without the caller noticing. Normalization is a rule for valid text, not a repair for corrupt bytes.

lessons.title: Collections that preserve your data
lessons.summary: Python in practice · lesson 2 of 5 · event-timeline repair
objectives: Preserve duplicates and stable ordering.
Choose counting and grouping tools deliberately.
Detect mismatched paired inputs.

exercises.title: Events disappear at the same timestamp
exercises.prompt: A report stores each event as events[timestamp] = record. Two events share the timestamp. Why does one disappear?
options: The second assignment replaces the value at the same key
hints: A dictionary holds one value per key.
Repeated events are valid input here.
Use a sequence if every record must remain.
exercises.solution: The second assignment overwrites the first value. Keep a list of events and sort it stably, so duplicate instants remain and ties preserve their original order.

exercises.title: Paired lists have different lengths
exercises.prompt: Names and scores must have equal lengths. How can you detect a mismatch while combining them?
options: Use ordinary zip and ignore the missing tail
Convert names to a set first
hints: Ordinary zip stops at the shorter input.
The check happens while iterating.
The strict option asks Python to reject a mismatch.
exercises.solution: Consume zip with strict=True. It raises ValueError if lengths differ. Merely creating the iterator does not finish the check; sorting independently can also break the association between a name and its score.

lessons.title: Dates, timestamps & input rules
lessons.summary: Python in practice · lesson 3 of 5 · event-timeline repair
objectives: Use calendar types for date arithmetic.
Distinguish naive and aware timestamps.
Validate offset requirements after parsing.

exercises.title: A timestamp has no offset
exercises.prompt: An event says 2024-06-01T09:00:00 and the lab requires an explicit offset. What should the parser do?
options: Reject it as missing offset information
hints: A clock reading alone may describe many instants.
The lab chooses rejection instead of guessing.
Parsing syntax is separate from checking the contract.
exercises.solution: Reject the naive value. A successful fromisoformat call does not prove the timestamp identifies the intended instant. Guessing a zone makes results depend on unstated assumptions.

exercises.title: Tomorrow at the end of February
exercises.prompt: How should code find the day after date(2024, 2, 28)?
options: Add one to a formatted date string
hints: The calendar rules depend on year and month.
Use a date operation rather than text manipulation.
2024 is a leap year.
exercises.solution: Add one day using timedelta. The date becomes 2024-02-29. Calendar arithmetic handles the month boundary and leap year; a text or fixed-length shortcut does not.

lessons.title: Time zones, conversion & elapsed time
lessons.summary: Python in practice · lesson 4 of 5 · event-timeline repair
objectives: Convert instants instead of relabelling them.
Distinguish fixed offsets and named-zone rules.
Choose clocks and arithmetic for elapsed time.

exercises.title: The event moved by five hours
exercises.prompt: Code converts 12:00+05:00 to UTC using replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc). Which result preserves the instant?
hints: Replace changes the label without adjusting the hour.
The source clock is five hours ahead of UTC.
Use conversion to preserve the instant.
exercises.solution: Use astimezone: noon at +05:00 is 07:00 UTC. Relabelling noon as UTC changes the instant instead of converting its display.

exercises.title: Timing a request while the system clock changes
exercises.prompt: Which clock is suitable for measuring elapsed work in the current process?
hints: Calendar clocks can be adjusted.
You need a difference, not a calendar date.
Use a clock intended for duration measurement.
exercises.solution: Use differences from perf_counter. It is intended for elapsed measurements and is monotonic. Its arbitrary starting point is not a timestamp you should store as a date.

lessons.title: Debug a broken event timeline
lessons.summary: Python in practice · lesson 5 of 5 · event-timeline repair
objectives: Reproduce a bug with minimal input.
Inspect values in a local debugger.
Repair the timeline and preserve regression tests.

exercises.title: A fix that cannot be reproduced
exercises.prompt: A bug disappears after a change, but no test captured it. What evidence should you add?
options: Delete the input that triggered it
A minimal regression test showing the former failure and expected behavior
A mock that returns the answer without running the code
hints: Preserve the contract and reproducing input.
The test should run the real failing path.
It must catch the mistake if someone reintroduces it.
exercises.solution: Keep a regression test using the smallest useful reproduction. Run the corrected code against the expected result. A comment or a mock of the function cannot detect the bug returning.

exercises.title: Inspect one transformation
exercises.prompt: The bytes decode but a label looks corrupted. Which debugging step gives useful evidence first?
options: Switch encodings randomly until no exception occurs
Inspect the raw bytes, decoding choice and repr of the resulting text
Change the expected label in the tests
hints: A successful decode can still use the wrong encoding.
Compare the value before and after the boundary.
Do not change the contract to match corrupted output.
exercises.solution: Inspect the bytes and the chosen decoding rule, then the resulting text with repr. That separates an encoding mistake from a later normalization bug and gives a concrete reproduction.

lessons.title: References, mutation & ownership
lessons.summary: Object semantics in concurrent services
objectives: Predict aliasing across function calls.
Choose copy boundaries deliberately.
Keep request-specific state out of shared objects.

exercises.title: A copy that still changes the original
exercises.prompt: After `a={"items": []}; b=a.copy(); b["items"].append(7)`, what is `a["items"]`?
hints: Separate the outer mapping from its values.
Which object does each `items` key reference?
dict.copy copies references to values.
exercises.solution: The result is [7]. Only the outer mapping was copied. Copy the nested list when that ownership boundary is intended, or use immutable tuples. A deep copy is unnecessary for this simple value.

exercises.title: The accumulating failure list
exercises.prompt: A function with `failures=[]` includes job IDs from previous calls, even without concurrent requests. What repair addresses the cause?
options: Restart the worker after each job
Default to None and allocate inside the function
hints: Reproduce using two sequential calls.
When is a default expression evaluated?
Allocate new request state per invocation.
exercises.solution: Use a None default and construct the list inside the function. Default expressions are evaluated at definition time, so the same list survives across calls. A lock serializes access but does not create a fresh list.

lessons.title: Classes, state & small interfaces
lessons.summary: Object design and typing · lesson 1 of 5 · objects that own their state
objectives: Keep instance and class state separate.
Use a property for derived data.
Return snapshots instead of exposing mutable state.

exercises.title: Two inboxes share one list
exercises.prompt: An Inbox class puts titles = [] in the class body. Two instances only call self.titles.append(...). Why do both show the same titles?
options: Both instances find the same class-owned list
hints: Find where the list is allocated.
Appending changes a list; it does not assign an instance attribute.
Allocate a new list in __init__ for each instance.
exercises.solution: Both instances find the one list stored on the class. Allocate self._titles = [] in __init__ so every inbox gets its own state. A lock would not make separate lists.

exercises.title: A count that cannot drift
exercises.prompt: An inbox exposes count and also supports adding and removing titles. How can count stay consistent without extra updates?
options: Store a second number and ask callers to maintain it
Compute count with a read-only property using the current list length
Return the mutable list to every caller
hints: Count is derived from existing state.
Two separate sources of truth can disagree.
A property can calculate a value when read.
exercises.solution: A property can return len(self._titles) every time count is read. That avoids a stored counter drifting after edits. Exposing the list would weaken the ownership boundary.

lessons.title: Dataclasses & dependable values
lessons.summary: Object design and typing · lesson 2 of 5 · values and validation
objectives: Use generated value equality.
Choose per-instance default factories.
Explain frozen fields and nested mutability.

exercises.title: Frozen around a mutable list
exercises.prompt: A frozen dataclass contains a list called labels. What happens when code calls item.labels.append("urgent")?
options: The list can change; frozen blocks ordinary field assignment
The list is automatically converted to a tuple
All nested values are deeply frozen
hints: Distinguish assigning a field from changing its value object.
The field still refers to the same list.
Choose immutable contained values when a stable snapshot matters.
exercises.solution: The list can change. Frozen blocks ordinary assignment to the field, but append mutates the existing list. A tuple of immutable elements is a better fit for this snapshot.

exercises.title: Fresh default drafts
exercises.prompt: A Draft dataclass needs an independent empty list of titles for every default instance. Which declaration fits?
options: One global list passed to all constructors
hints: A factory is called when a default is needed.
Pass the function, not its result.
list makes a fresh empty list when called.
exercises.solution: field(default_factory=list) calls list separately for each default. list() is already a list, not a factory. A caller-supplied list can still be shared; the factory does not copy explicit inputs.

lessons.title: Composition & replaceable helpers
lessons.summary: Object design and typing · lesson 3 of 5 · services and storage
objectives: Pass dependencies through constructors.
Choose composition when a service uses a helper.
Validate before performing writes.

exercises.title: A service is not its database
exercises.prompt: A task service validates input and uses a store. Which design makes storage replaceable without claiming the service is a store?
options: Receive a store in the service constructor and delegate writes
Use a global store hidden inside every method
Copy the database implementation into the service
hints: The relationship is uses, not a new kind of store.
Let the caller supply the collaborator.
The service owns validation; the store owns persistence.
exercises.solution: Pass the store to the constructor and keep it as a collaborator. This is composition. The caller can supply a memory store or fake without a storage inheritance hierarchy.

exercises.title: A rejected call left a task
exercises.prompt: A service saves a task, then checks whether the title is blank. A rejected request remains in storage. What directly repairs the sequence?
options: Hide the error from the caller
Validate and construct the task before calling the store
Add a type annotation to the title only
hints: An invalid request should cause no write.
A type hint does not enforce the nonblank rule.
Move the decision before the side effect.
exercises.solution: Validate the full input first and write only after it is accepted. Type annotations cannot enforce this runtime rule. Retrying an invalid write or hiding the error leaves the bad state behind.

lessons.title: Type hints & runtime input checks
lessons.summary: Object design and typing · lesson 4 of 5 · types and boundary checks
objectives: Narrow unknown values with runtime checks.
Handle unions and readable collection interfaces.
Run mypy separately from runtime tests.

exercises.title: A number arrives for a typed title
exercises.prompt: A JSON client sends title=42 to code annotated title: str. What actually protects the task title boundary?
options: The annotation automatically converts 42 to text
A runtime check rejecting non-string and blank values
A cast to str that proves the value is text
hints: Hints describe intended calls.
Outside input may violate the description.
Check type and business rules before building the value.
exercises.solution: Use runtime checks before constructing the task. The annotation and cast do not validate incoming data; neither converts the number. A checker helps callers in checked source, while validation protects outside input.

exercises.title: An empty result is still possible
exercises.prompt: first_title returns str | None. Before using .upper() on its result, what should the caller do?
options: Assume the list is never empty
Change the return type to Any
Handle None and only call upper on the string branch
Catch every exception and return an empty string
hints: The return type includes an absence case.
Use a local variable to inspect that result.
An explicit None check narrows the remaining branch.
exercises.solution: Handle None explicitly, then call upper on the string. The union records a real possibility; hiding it behind Any or swallowing all errors loses useful information.

lessons.title: Protocols, fakes & the typed task inbox
lessons.summary: Object design and typing · lesson 5 of 5 · typed project evidence
objectives: Describe the smallest useful storage interface.
Test the real service with recording and failing fakes.
Separate runtime, static and reviewer evidence.

exercises.title: A matching store without inheritance
exercises.prompt: RecordingStore has compatible add and all methods but does not inherit TaskStore. Can a type checker accept it for a TaskStore parameter?
options: No, every protocol needs explicit inheritance
Yes, compatible operations can satisfy the protocol structurally
Yes, even if its return types are incompatible
hints: Protocols describe operations.
Compare signatures as well as method names.
Inheritance is optional for this structural match.
exercises.solution: Yes. Compatible method signatures can satisfy the protocol without inheritance. Names alone are not enough, and this type check does not prove that the methods persist tasks correctly.

exercises.title: The test skipped validation
exercises.prompt: A test replaces TaskService.create with a mock returning a Task. It claims invalid input cannot be stored. What should the test exercise instead?
options: The same mock with a different return value
The real service with an injected recording store and invalid input
A screenshot of a green type check
hints: The replaced method contained the behavior under test.
Replace the dependency, not the validation logic.
Assert no write was recorded for rejected input.
exercises.solution: Call the real service with invalid input and a recording fake store. Assert an error and no writes. A mocked create method skips validation; a clean type check alone cannot prove the ordering of side effects.

lessons.title: Iterables, iterators & one-pass input
lessons.summary: Generators and resource cleanup · lesson 1 of 5
objectives: Distinguish a collection from its iterator.
Predict consumption and exhaustion.
Process a one-use source in one pass.

exercises.title: The second pass is empty
exercises.prompt: A cursor is created with iter(["api", "db"]). After list(cursor) returns both names, what does another list(cursor) return?
hints: An iterator remembers its current position.
The first conversion consumed its remaining values.
A consumed iterator does not reset itself.
exercises.solution: The second list is empty because the cursor is exhausted. Keep the original collection or create a fresh source if replay is required. Calling iter on the same iterator does not restart it.

exercises.title: Count and last from one source
exercises.prompt: A function counts an iterator, then loops over it again to find its last value. It works for lists but fails for file-like sources. Which fix supports both?
options: Call iter twice on the same cursor
Count and update the last value in the same loop
Catch every exception and return zero
hints: The source might support only one pass.
Keep both small pieces of state together.
One loop can update count and last for every item.
exercises.solution: Update count and last in a single pass, with a separate empty-input result. Reusing the same cursor cannot replay consumed values. A global value would also leak state between calls.

lessons.title: Generators & deferred work
lessons.summary: Generators and resource cleanup · lesson 2 of 5
objectives: Predict when a generator body runs.
Handle errors during consumption.
Verify laziness as well as output.

exercises.title: A created parser has not validated the file
exercises.prompt: A generator parses one line before each yield. Creating it succeeds. Its third line is malformed. When should the caller expect that parsing failure?
options: At the third request for a record
Only after a new Python process starts
hints: Calling a generator function does not run its body.
Advancing it runs work up to the next yield or failure.
Put handling around the consuming operation.
exercises.solution: The failure arrives when consumption reaches the third line. Creating a generator is not proof the input is valid. Catch expected parsing failures around the loop or consumer, not only around construction.

exercises.title: Testing a lazy running total
exercises.prompt: A running-total generator produces the right final list but reads the entire source before its first yield. Which test exposes this?
options: Compare only the final list again
Use a recording source and verify one next consumes only one input
Check the function name contains generator
hints: Correct values do not prove consumption timing.
Observe requests to the source.
Check construction and the first advancement separately.
exercises.solution: A recording source reveals when inputs are requested. Construction should consume nothing and the first output should require only the first input here. Comparing final values alone misses eager materialization.

lessons.title: Streaming pipelines & memory limits
lessons.summary: Generators and resource cleanup · lesson 3 of 5
objectives: Track state retained by every stage.
Bound individual line reads.
Separate complete success from partial consumption.

exercises.title: The generator that still fills memory
exercises.prompt: A source yields records lazily, but its consumer calls sorted(source) before producing output. Why can memory still grow with the file?
options: Yield permanently caps memory for every downstream function
sorted collects the input before returning its sorted list
All generators secretly copy the file
Integer arithmetic always loads the source
hints: Inspect the consumer, not just the producer.
Global sorting needs the values it will order.
A lazy first stage does not make every stage lazy.
exercises.solution: sorted collects the input into a list for sorting. A lazy producer cannot prevent that downstream allocation. Choose a bounded aggregation or external sorting when the full collection cannot fit.

exercises.title: One enormous log line
exercises.prompt: A line-by-line reader receives a single 100 MB line. What limits memory before parsing under the lab contract?
options: Read the full line and then check its size
Read at most limit + 1 bytes and reject an oversized record
hints: A whole line can be much larger than normal records.
Checking only after an unbounded read is too late.
One extra byte detects overflow without loading the remainder.
exercises.solution: A bounded readline(limit + 1) distinguishes a valid maximum-length line from an oversized one. Reject it before collecting the rest. Line-by-line iteration alone does not bound the size of a line.

lessons.title: Useful exceptions & preserved causes
lessons.summary: Generators and resource cleanup · lesson 4 of 5
objectives: Add a one-based record position to expected errors.
Preserve the original exception cause.
Avoid hiding failures during cleanup.

exercises.title: Keep the decoding failure visible
exercises.prompt: A parser catches UnicodeDecodeError as exc and wants to raise RecordError with a line number while retaining the cause. Which form fits?
hints: Add context without erasing the lower-level reason.
Exception chaining records an explicit cause.
The from expression should refer to the caught error.
exercises.solution: Use raise RecordError(message) from exc. Callers get useful line context and the traceback retains the decoding cause. Returning an empty record would turn failed input into apparent success.

exercises.title: A cleanup block swallowed an error
exercises.prompt: A function raises RecordError, but its finally block returns an empty report. Why does the caller see success?
options: The return in finally replaces the pending exception
hints: Finally executes while an exception is leaving the block.
A new return changes that control flow.
Cleanup should not return a fake successful value.
exercises.solution: The return in finally suppresses the pending error. Remove that return and let the exception propagate after cleanup. Otherwise a failed parse becomes a misleading empty report.

lessons.title: Context managers & the streaming log lab
lessons.summary: Generators and resource cleanup · lesson 5 of 5
objectives: Make ownership and cleanup scopes explicit.

Keep borrowed sources under caller ownership.

exercises.title: Break with a retained generator

Wait until the process eventually stops
hints: Stopping iteration is not the same as closing it.
A retained generator may stay paused with its local state.
Make lifetime a visible responsibility.
exercises.solution: Use an explicit context scope that closes the owned file and generator on exit. A loop break alone does not promise this cleanup, and type hints do not release resources.

exercises.title: Who closes the borrowed stream?

Raise the contextual error and leave source closure to its owner
hints: The parser did not acquire the resource.
Read the ownership contract separately from validation rules.
The enclosing owner must arrange cleanup.
exercises.solution: Raise the useful parsing error and leave the borrowed source open. The caller owns its lifetime. open_readings is the separate context manager that acquires and closes its own file.

Collect bounded line bytes, then decode the complete line

exercises.solution: Register cleanup after each handoff. Failure cannot convert a partial setup into success.

lessons.title: Profile the same stated workload
lessons.summary: Compare equivalent outputs with stated cache state, actual timings, profiles and Python allocation observations.
objectives: Compare equivalent outputs with stated cache state, actual timings, profiles and Python allocation observations.

Implement analyse, then run the installed demo on both stated distributions. Preserve ordered outputs. Explain cProfile calls and cumulative time, Python allocation limits, fresh cache state and why the cyclic distribution gets no hits. Add a different independent workload.
Include actual JSON and command output. Do not invent a speedup or use a fixed millisecond threshold. Separate service collection, CPU reporting, worker ownership and instrumented observations.

exercises.title: Practical boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: An eight-entry LRU sees 32 distinct keys in order, then the same 32 again. What evidence should you expect?
options: Every second request is a hit
The reuse distance can evict each key before reuse
The cache grows to 32 entries automatically
hints: Identify the input, result and resource owner.
Separate finite checks from the judgment still needed.
Compare equivalent outputs with stated cache state, actual timings, profiles and Python allocation observations.
exercises.solution: Each key returns after 31 other keys; capacity eight cannot retain it in this cycle.

exercises.title: Practical boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: The candidate preserves outputs and makes fewer calls, but one timing sample is slower. What should the reviewer do?
options: Interpret all raw samples and scope without a universal speed gate
Change the expected output to favor the cache
hints: Identify the input, result and resource owner.
Separate finite checks from the judgment still needed.
Compare equivalent outputs with stated cache state, actual timings, profiles and Python allocation observations.
exercises.solution: Behavior/counts are contracts; timing varies with workload and environment and needs interpretation.

lessons.title: Preserve callers while changing internals
lessons.summary: Keep old HTTP, value, warning and ownership contracts while comparing a new implementation.

Run the installed caller and service regressions. Choose an independent proposed change, list the supported behaviors it may affect, and add a before/after regression that fails for an incompatible implementation. Include warning and cleanup evidence.
Keep old packages byte-for-byte unchanged. Explain what the service_002 rehearsal establishes and why later release/database units keep their separate contracts and histories.

exercises.title: Practical boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: A deprecated public function still has supported callers. May the candidate silently remove its documented warning to keep logs quiet?
options: Yes, warnings are not observable behavior
No; preserve warning and return semantics for supported callers
Only if the cache has a hit
hints: Identify the input, result and resource owner.
Separate finite checks from the judgment still needed.
Keep old HTTP, value, warning and ownership contracts while comparing a new implementation.
exercises.solution: The documented warning is part of compatibility. Catch and record an expected warning explicitly.

exercises.title: Practical boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: Strict installed typing passes. Does that prove a webhook caller is authorized or a transaction committed?
options: No; those require runtime authority and storage evidence
Yes, if every field has a type
Yes, if the package has py.typed
hints: Identify the input, result and resource owner.
Separate finite checks from the judgment still needed.
Keep old HTTP, value, warning and ownership contracts while comparing a new implementation.
exercises.solution: Static contracts and runtime security/storage behavior answer different questions.

lessons.title: Submit an original practical-review artifact
lessons.summary: Present an independently designed case, installed evidence and a versioned manual-review explanation.
objectives: Present an independently designed case, installed evidence and a versioned manual-review explanation.

Create and run an independent case plus regression, write the decision note, and attach the exact revision and installed report. Submit a fixed artifact for manual review. Respond to one concrete review finding in a preserved revision.
Check ownership, uncertainty and measurement limits in your explanation. Label assessor examples and reported evidence accurately; do not imply that the academy ran your uploaded package.

exercises.title: Practical boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: The data-only case checker passes and reports output equivalence. What still needs a reviewer?
options: Whether the case is original, useful and well explained
The existence of the JSON file
hints: Identify the input, result and resource owner.
Separate finite checks from the judgment still needed.
Present an independently designed case, installed evidence and a versioned manual-review explanation.
exercises.solution: Finite claims can be checked. Originality, tradeoffs and adequacy need independent judgment.

exercises.title: Practical boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: A learner saves successful test output and a checklist. What does the platform record?
options: Reported/manual evidence without automatic practical mastery
hints: Identify the input, result and resource owner.
Separate finite checks from the judgment still needed.
Present an independently designed case, installed evidence and a versioned manual-review explanation.
exercises.solution: Self/human review and reported tests remain separate from objective mastery.

lessons.title: Transactions that survive concurrency
lessons.summary: MVCC, conditional writes & row locks
objectives: Explain why read-then-write can oversell.
Choose an atomic update or row lock.
Define the worker claim transaction boundary.

exercises.title: The last item is sold twice
exercises.prompt: Two transactions read stock=1 then each unconditionally writes stock=0 and creates an order. Which change directly protects one-unit reservation?
options: Wrap the same code in a transaction
Use an atomic decrement WHERE available > 0 and check RETURNING
Cache stock in Redis for one minute
hints: Which statement enforces the business condition?
Can another writer change stock after the read?
Combine the decision and mutation.
exercises.solution: Use a conditional UPDATE and create the order only when a row is returned, in the same transaction. The second writer rechecks the condition after waiting and cannot reserve unavailable stock. A prior SELECT alone is not an invariant.

exercises.title: The vanished worker
exercises.prompt: A worker claims a job with SKIP LOCKED, marks it running, commits, then crashes. What is still required?
options: Nothing: row locks restore pending status after commit
A lease expiry/reaper and idempotent processing
A longer lock held during all HTTP calls
hints: The claim transaction already committed.
Who notices a running job with no worker?
Recover expired claims while tolerating duplicate effects.
exercises.solution: Committed running state survives the crash. Track a lease and recover abandoned claims; make processing idempotent because a stale worker can resume after its lease expires. SKIP LOCKED prevents competing row claims, not all duplicate execution.

lessons.title: When the response never arrives
lessons.summary: Idempotency keys, retries & uncertain outcomes
objectives: Distinguish failure from an unknown outcome.
Bind idempotency keys to payloads and owners.
Design bounded retries.

exercises.title: A committed payment, a lost response
exercises.prompt: The client times out after the payment committed. What should its retry preserve?
options: A new random key per HTTP attempt
The original operation key and request body
hints: Transport attempt and business operation are different identities.
The server needs to recognize the same intended action.
Keep the operation key stable across retries.
exercises.solution: Reuse the original key and identical payload. The server returns the stored outcome or reconciles an in-progress operation. A fresh key tells the server this may be a new business operation.

exercises.title: Same key, different amount
exercises.prompt: A caller reuses a completed payment key but changes amount from 10 to 100. What response preserves the contract?
options: Delete the old key and proceed
hints: The key represents one intended operation.
Silent reuse can hide a client bug.
Compare a canonical request fingerprint.
exercises.solution: Reject the conflicting reuse, commonly with 409. Scope the record to caller and operation, and compare a canonical request hash. Replaying without validation hides errors; creating a new payment defeats the key contract.

lessons.title: The crash between commit and ack
lessons.summary: At-least-once delivery & safe consumers
objectives: Predict broker redelivery after a crash.
Place deduplication in the business transaction.
Explain effectively-once effects.

exercises.title: Commit succeeds; ack never happens
exercises.prompt: A worker commits an invoice then dies before broker acknowledgement. What is the expected risk with at-least-once delivery?
options: The broker must know the SQL transaction committed
The event may be delivered again
The invoice is automatically rolled back
hints: The broker and database keep separate state.
Which operation told the broker to forget the delivery?
There was no acknowledgement.
exercises.solution: The broker may redeliver. Protect invoice creation with a stable unique event/business identifier and acknowledge only after the transaction commits. The database does not roll back an already committed transaction because the worker died.

exercises.title: The misleading dedup marker
exercises.prompt: A consumer commits a consumed-event marker, then starts a second transaction for the ledger update. What failure can lose work?
options: The ledger transaction fails but the marker remains
The marker has a primary key
hints: Consider a crash between the two transactions.
How will redelivery interpret the marker?
Deduplication and effect must commit together.
exercises.solution: If the second transaction fails, the durable marker can make redelivery skip an effect that never happened. Put the marker and ledger write in one transaction. For external effects, use an explicit additional idempotency/reconciliation boundary.

lessons.title: One transaction, two intentions
lessons.summary: The transactional outbox without mythology
objectives: Remove the dual-write gap.
Explain why relay duplicates remain possible.
Choose when an outbox is unnecessary.

exercises.title: A silent fulfillment gap
exercises.prompt: Order commit succeeds but event publication fails. Which design preserves the intent atomically with the order?
options: Write an outbox row in the order transaction
Retry publication only in process memory
hints: Both durable facts must share a commit boundary.
An in-memory retry disappears on restart.
Store publication intent alongside the order.
exercises.solution: Insert an outbox row in the same database transaction. A relay can later publish it. Publishing first can create phantom events; in-memory retry state is lost on crashes.

exercises.title: The relay publishes twice
exercises.prompt: A relay publishes successfully and crashes before marking sent. What should the design assume?
options: The consumer must tolerate a repeated event ID
The order transaction is rolled back
The relay must generate a new event ID
hints: Publication and marking sent are separate commits.
Retrying the row is necessary to avoid loss.
Keep the original event identity.
exercises.solution: Assume duplicate publication and deduplicate the business effect using the stable event ID. An outbox guarantees durable publication intent, not single delivery. A new ID on retry defeats consumer deduplication.

lessons.title: Keep the request boundary thin
lessons.summary: Validation, services & transaction ownership
objectives: Separate transport validation from domain invariants.
Assign one transaction owner.
Recognize blocking I/O in async endpoints.

exercises.title: Async in name only
exercises.prompt: An `async def` route calls a blocking HTTP client for 3 seconds. Other requests stall. What addresses the event-loop problem?
options: Add another await before the blocking call
Use an async client or offload the blocking operation appropriately
Put the call in a Pydantic validator
hints: async def does not rewrite the called library.
What thread runs the blocking operation?
Use a nonblocking client or a worker/thread boundary.
exercises.solution: Use an async HTTP client, or an appropriate thread offload/synchronous route for the blocking stack. Declaring a function async alone does not make blocking I/O cooperative.

exercises.title: Two repositories, half an order
exercises.prompt: InventoryRepository commits before OrderRepository fails. What boundary change prevents partial success?
options: Let the use case own one transaction across both writes
Return HTTP 200 on the second error
hints: Which caller understands the full business operation?
A committed first write cannot be rolled back by the second repository.
Helpers may flush; the use case decides commit.
exercises.solution: One use-case transaction should contain reservation and order creation. Repositories can flush but must not commit independently. A successful response or caught exception cannot undo a previous commit.

lessons.title: A queue is a failure boundary
lessons.summary: Acknowledgements, retries & cache limits
objectives: Choose acknowledgement timing.
Bound retry amplification.
Distinguish caches from authoritative state.

exercises.title: The message that never gets better
exercises.prompt: A malformed event fails identically on every retry and dominates the queue. What should change?
options: Classify permanent failures and quarantine with alerting
Acknowledge all future events before parsing
hints: Will time make an invalid schema valid?
Retries consume the same scarce capacity.
Separate transient and permanent errors.
exercises.solution: Quarantine permanent failures with metadata, alerting and a repair/replay process. Infinite immediate retry creates a poison-message loop. More workers can amplify the same failure.

exercises.title: A lock holder wakes up late
exercises.prompt: Worker A pauses longer than its Redis lock TTL. B acquires the lock, then A resumes. Which statement is correct?
options: A cannot run because the TTL expired
Both can execute; the downstream invariant needs protection
hints: The lease is remote state, not a process kill switch.
What prevents A from issuing its next write?
Use downstream checks such as fencing or a database constraint.
exercises.solution: Both workers can execute. Lease expiration does not stop A. Use an appropriate downstream invariant or fencing protocol; token-checked lock release alone only prevents deleting another owner’s lock.

lessons.title: Containers that shut down safely
lessons.summary: Signals, readiness & deployment boundaries
objectives: Distinguish process startup from readiness.
Propagate shutdown signals.
Plan compatible database rollouts.

exercises.title: It works inside the container
exercises.prompt: Uvicorn binds to 127.0.0.1 inside a container. Another Compose service cannot connect. What should change?
options: Bind the server to 0.0.0.0 inside the container
hints: Each container has its own network namespace.
Loopback belongs to that container.
Listen on the container network interface.
exercises.solution: Bind to 0.0.0.0 and connect using the Compose service name and container port. Host port publishing is separate. Another container’s localhost points to itself.

exercises.title: A rollout breaks old replicas
exercises.prompt: A new release immediately drops a column still read by old replicas. What deployment strategy avoids this incompatibility?
options: Expand, deploy compatible code, backfill, then contract
Run DROP COLUMN from every replica
hints: Two application versions coexist during a rollout.
Schema changes need a compatibility window.
Separate additive changes from destructive cleanup.
exercises.solution: Use expand-and-contract with a deliberate compatibility window. Destructive cleanup follows deployment and verification that no old reader remains. Rollback plans must account for schema compatibility too.

lessons.title: A model response is a proposal
lessons.summary: Structured output, uncertainty & application contracts
objectives: Separate syntactic validity from truth.
Budget context and latency.
Define failure handling for model output.

exercises.title: Valid JSON, invalid expense
exercises.prompt: A model emits schema-valid JSON with another tenant’s account ID. What is still required?
options: Trust it because structured output was enabled
Authorize the account against the authenticated principal
Add the tenant ID to the prompt only
hints: Shape and permission answer different questions.
Which component knows the authenticated user?
Application code must enforce access control.
exercises.solution: Authorize the proposed account against the authenticated principal in application code. A schema constrains structure, not ownership or factual correctness. Prompt instructions are not an authorization boundary.

exercises.title: Temperature zero as a guarantee
exercises.prompt: A team claims temperature=0 proves responses are correct and permanently reproducible. What is the best correction?
options: It only works if responses are longer
Reduced sampling variability is not a truth or stability guarantee
It guarantees correctness but not JSON
hints: Separate randomness from correctness.
Can a consistently generated claim still be false?
Evaluate the behavior of the actual model and version.
exercises.solution: Lower variability does not establish truth, and model/infrastructure changes can alter output. Use versioned evaluation datasets, explicit validation and recorded model versions. Some models do not expose the same sampling controls.

lessons.title: Keep provider configuration outside user text
lessons.summary: Pin the provider, model, prompt and schema; treat generated text as a proposal.

Record what the protocol checks statically, what runtime validation checks, and what a fake cannot establish. Do not claim that a role label alone prevents prompt injection.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: A ticket says to change the provider ID and use a privileged model. Where should the selected adapter come from?
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Pin the provider, model, prompt and schema; treat generated text as a proposal.
exercises.solution: The application configures adapters and authority. User or generated text cannot select privileged capabilities.

options: Accept it if the summary is fluent
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Pin the provider, model, prompt and schema; treat generated text as a proposal.
exercises.solution: Reject unexpected identity. Record the configured model/prompt/schema so a supported run is reproducible.

lessons.title: Reserve context before sending a request

exercises.prompt: A context check counts just the ticket body and ignores instructions, schema and output reserve. What is missing?
options: The full supported request envelope and output allocation
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Count the full configured envelope and leave room for output; reject overflow explicitly.
exercises.solution: Admission must account for the complete supported input envelope plus output. The lab uses a stated byte fixture, not real tokenization.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: The byte fixture passes for a request. What can you conclude about a real provider tokenizer?
options: Its actual token count is identical
Nothing without a verified model-specific counter and overhead policy
The provider can never reject context
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Count the full configured envelope and leave room for output; reject overflow explicitly.
exercises.solution: Fixture counts are exact only for this invented rule. Real tokenization, framing and capabilities need separate verification.

lessons.title: Separate complete, refused and incomplete output

Implement decode_reply for both exact formats. Test complete/refused/incomplete, duplicate keys, wrong revision, mixed fields, fenced JSON, extra authority fields and string booleans. Keep non-complete Decisions absent.
Demonstrate that an accepted object can still be wrong or unauthorized. The decoder must not execute or treat generated fields as authority.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: A truncated provider result contains the beginning of a valid triage object. What is safe for this contract?
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Normalize provider variants, validate exact proposal fields, and keep refusal/partial text out of actions.
exercises.solution: Partial output is a distinct non-complete outcome. Do not create a business proposal from an unfinished prefix.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: A proposal contains needs_human as the string "false". What should strict validation do?
options: Coerce any nonempty string to true
Treat it as an exact JSON boolean
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Normalize provider variants, validate exact proposal fields, and keep refusal/partial text out of actions.
exercises.solution: Use current exact boolean validation. Strings, numbers and missing fields are different inputs.

lessons.title: Keep cancellation and timeout outcomes honest
lessons.summary: Use one shrinking cooperative deadline and await cleanup; an uncertain call is not a free or rolled-back call.
objectives: Use one shrinking cooperative deadline and await cleanup; an uncertain call is not a free or rolled-back call.
Run the waiting timeout and external-cancellation fixtures. Verify entered/finished events, propagated cancellation, borrowed transport reuse and a shrinking deadline across calls.
Do not claim that cooperative cleanup rolls back remote effects or that timeout means zero usage. State the absence of a durable cancellation ledger and hard interruption.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: A three-call run gives each call the original full timeout. What is wrong with a shared total waiting policy?
options: It can expand the total budget; use a single shrinking deadline
It always closes the transport too early
It proves the provider did no work
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Use one shrinking cooperative deadline and await cleanup; an uncertain call is not a free or rolled-back call.
exercises.solution: Keep one deadline and calculate remaining time. Cleanup and blocking work still require honest cooperative limits.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: The caller times out without metering. Which statement is supported?
options: The provider definitely used zero units
The outcome and usage may be unknown
All remote effects were rolled back
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Use one shrinking cooperative deadline and await cleanup; an uncertain call is not a free or rolled-back call.
exercises.solution: Timeout limits waiting, not remote work. Retain uncertain accounting and do not infer rollback or zero usage.

lessons.title: Reserve cost and count attempts before calls
lessons.summary: Admit work before sending it, settle known bounded usage, and keep unknown usage reserved.
objectives: Admit work before sending it, settle known bounded usage, and keep unknown usage reserved.
Implement async run. Test reserve-minus-one refusal/no call, exact-reserve admission, later settlement and next-call gating, actual attempt limits, zero rates and full reservations for unknown usage.
Report fictional rates and fixture units explicitly. Show no request was made when admission failed; explain why the ledger is not durable billing or an account quota.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: The remaining fictional budget is one credit below the next full reservation. What should happen?
options: Call first and hope output is short
Make no provider call and stop at cost_limit
Charge only after every prompt finishes
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Admit work before sending it, settle known bounded usage, and keep unknown usage reserved.
exercises.solution: Admission must precede the call. A reservation that cannot fit blocks work even if its eventual usage might be smaller.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: A malformed reply prevents full usage validation after a call. How does this local ledger settle?
options: Release all credits as if no work occurred
Keep the full reservation and stop
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Admit work before sending it, settle known bounded usage, and keep unknown usage reserved.
exercises.solution: Unknown usage is not free. This lab keeps the reservation and stops rather than inventing billing certainty.

lessons.title: Review model contracts without inventing model quality
lessons.summary: Install outside source, preserve versions and failures, and separate fixture evidence from real model behavior.
objectives: Install outside source, preserve versions and failures, and separate fixture evidence from real model behavior.
Install the completed wheel outside source, save the demo JSON and add an independent regression plus decision note. Submit a fixed artifact and preserve one revision responding to feedback.
Label the report as fixture/application evidence. Do not present fake counts as provider conformance, billing correctness, factual quality or expertise.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 1
exercises.prompt: All scripted adapter cases pass. Which claim is justified?
options: The exercised finite application contracts pass
Every real provider returns correct answers
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Install outside source, preserve versions and failures, and separate fixture evidence from real model behavior.
exercises.solution: Scripted fixtures establish only the application boundaries they exercised. They do not run or certify a real model or invoice.

exercises.title: Model boundary check 2
exercises.prompt: A submission contains successful fake output but omits the model/prompt/schema versions and failure cases. What should review request?
options: Versioned installed artifacts and explicit failure/limit evidence
hints: Identify which application boundary the case actually evaluates.
Distinguish an attempted call from a useful result and known usage.
Install outside source, preserve versions and failures, and separate fixture evidence from real model behavior.
exercises.solution: Reproducible boundaries and failure evidence make the review meaningful. Keep reported/manual evidence separate from mastery.

lessons.title: Similarity is not relevance
lessons.summary: Chunking, filters & measurable retrieval
objectives: Distinguish geometric similarity from relevance.
Preserve meaning across chunk boundaries.
Apply authorization before returning candidates.

exercises.title: An exception in another chunk
exercises.prompt: Retrieval repeatedly finds a refund rule but misses its exception in the next chunk. What experiment targets the failure?
options: Compare structure-aware chunking with boundary-focused labeled queries
hints: The missing evidence exists, but the representation separated it.
Create queries that need the rule and exception together.
Measure retrieval after changing chunk boundaries.
exercises.solution: Test structure-aware chunks or suitable overlap against boundary-specific queries. Measure recall and answer support. Generation settings cannot reliably recover evidence that was never retrieved.

exercises.title: The reranker cannot see it
exercises.prompt: A relevant document is absent from the top 50 candidates. Can reranking only those 50 recover it?
options: Yes, reranking searches the entire corpus
No; improve candidate recall before reranking
Only if the document is private
hints: What inputs does this reranker receive?
Ranking changes order within the supplied set.
Candidate generation and ranking are separate stages.
exercises.solution: No. A reranker can reorder only the candidates it receives. Improve retrieval recall through query strategy, filters, hybrid search, chunking or candidate depth, then measure whether reranking improves precision.

lessons.title: Keep chunks connected to their source
lessons.summary: Preserve tenant, document, revision, ordinal, character offsets and text digest.
objectives: Preserve tenant, document, revision, ordinal, character offsets and text digest.
Implement make_chunks. Verify exact slices, Unicode offsets, overlap, final-tail behavior and stable complete keys. Show that changing revision changes identity without mutating the input.
Explain which chunking choice you measured and which source-lifecycle assumptions remain supplied by the application.

exercises.title: Retrieval check 1
exercises.prompt: Two tenants have document ID guide and chunk ordinal 0. What identifies a chunk?
options: Tenant, document, revision and ordinal together
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Preserve tenant, document, revision, ordinal, character offsets and text digest.
exercises.solution: Use a complete scoped key. Document IDs and positions can repeat across tenants and revisions.

exercises.title: Retrieval check 2
exercises.prompt: The final window already reaches the source end. What happens next?
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Preserve tenant, document, revision, ordinal, character offsets and text digest.
exercises.solution: Stop at the end. Preserve the exact source slice and avoid an unnecessary repeated tail.

lessons.title: Match vector model, version and dimensions
lessons.summary: Reject incompatible, non-finite and zero-norm vectors before ranking.
objectives: Reject incompatible, non-finite and zero-norm vectors before ranking.
Validate model/version/dimensions and finite nonzero vectors. Add a wrong-model regression with matching dimensions, and test scale, negative scores and zero rejection.
State why the hand-supplied vectors and a cosine score cannot establish real embedding-model quality.

exercises.title: Retrieval check 1
exercises.prompt: Two models both produce six numbers. Can their vectors be mixed?
options: Only with a verified shared model/version contract
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Reject incompatible, non-finite and zero-norm vectors before ranking.
exercises.solution: Length alone does not identify a vector space. This lab rejects any Spec mismatch.

exercises.title: Retrieval check 2
exercises.prompt: A passage has cosine score 1. What does that prove?
options: Directions align in the stated vector space
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Reject incompatible, non-finite and zero-norm vectors before ranking.
exercises.solution: Cosine measures vector direction. It does not grant access or prove truth/relevance.

lessons.title: Check access before scoring or taking top results
lessons.summary: Select the latest scoped revision, then enforce tenant, activity, groups and metadata.
objectives: Select the latest scoped revision, then enforce tenant, activity, groups and metadata.
Implement retrieve using supplied eligible validation. Test a closest private hit, another tenant, latest-private/old-public revisions, inactive updates and metadata filters before scoring.
Explain trusted principal ownership and the complete-current-corpus assumption. Do not claim an entire production authorization system is verified.

exercises.title: Retrieval check 1
exercises.prompt: Revision 1 is public; revision 2 is private. A public user searches. Which revision may return?
options: Revision 2 if its score is high
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Select the latest scoped revision, then enforce tenant, activity, groups and metadata.
exercises.solution: Determine current revision before access filtering. A restricted current revision must not reopen an old public version.

exercises.title: Retrieval check 2
exercises.prompt: A forbidden chunk would rank first. When must its access be checked?
options: Before scoring and before top k
Only when an answer cites it
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Select the latest scoped revision, then enforce tenant, activity, groups and metadata.
exercises.solution: Filter eligible candidates before scoring; then select top k from that set.

lessons.title: Compare exact vector ranking with a keyword baseline

Install outside source, save computed reports and add an independently explained regression.

hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.

Install outside source, save computed reports and add an independently explained regression.

Bind citations to retrieved spans.
Carry access control through the full pipeline.

Who originally generated this cached answer?
Include authorization context in every reuse boundary.

Identify the earliest boundary with incorrect output.
Inspect how generation used the evidence.
exercises.solution: Investigate generation, conflicting instructions, context interpretation and support checks. Retrieval tuning might help other failures, but this trace already shows relevant evidence in context. Use the trace to localize the defect.

Explain why deletion needs a retained revision and what the local SQLite experiment does not prove about distributed ingestion or production PostgreSQL.

Replace whole document revisions atomically and prevent old content from returning.

exercises.title: Evidence check 2
exercises.prompt: A deleted document receives a delayed old publication. What prevents its return?

A retained deletion marker with its newer revision
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Replace whole document revisions atomically and prevent old content from returning.
exercises.solution: Retain the current deletion revision. Old messages must not recreate removed content.

lessons.title: Select and pack whole authorized evidence

exercises.title: Evidence check 1
exercises.prompt: A private passage scores highest. May a reranker place it in context?

No; access must already exclude it

Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Separate candidate retrieval, an explicit task gate, reranking and byte-bounded context.

exercises.title: Evidence check 2

Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Separate candidate retrieval, an explicit task gate, reranking and byte-bounded context.
exercises.solution: Preserve whole source chunks. Silent truncation can change meaning and break the stated citation contract.

lessons.title: Bind citations to selected source excerpts

Validate a complete response with at most two whole-excerpt claims, distinct selected IDs and no extra fields. Bind citations to exact source spans and resolve them under current permissions.
Separate exact provenance, semantic support and source truth. No generated URL or citation ID can authorize a source or a business action.

exercises.title: Evidence check 1

Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.

exercises.title: Evidence check 2

hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Validate proposed IDs and exact whole quotes before constructing visible text.
exercises.solution: Exact source identity is measurable. Truth, usefulness and freeform entailment need separate evidence.

lessons.title: Abstain when evidence or generation is unusable

Explain why similarity, shape and abstention policy are separate from calibrated confidence, real billing and factual answer quality.

exercises.title: Evidence check 1
exercises.prompt: No whole evidence passage survives the configured policy. Should the lab call generation anyway?
options: Yes to invent a plausible answer
Only for a more fluent refusal

Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Use zero-call missing-evidence handling and separate unsupported, refused, incomplete and failed output.

exercises.title: Evidence check 2

hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Use zero-call missing-evidence handling and separate unsupported, refused, incomplete and failed output.
exercises.solution: Output support and measured usage are different boundaries. Reject the answer without inventing zero usage.

lessons.title: Refresh permissions and sources after generation

exercises.title: Evidence check 1

Ask the model to assign a role

Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Discard a prepared answer when authority, document state or the source epoch changes.

exercises.title: Evidence check 2

options: Discard the stale answer and citations
hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Discard a prepared answer when authority, document state or the source epoch changes.
exercises.solution: Recheck current source state after generation. A prior valid quote cannot override a newer deletion.

lessons.title: Review RAG evidence with honest quality limits

Build/install all three completed wheels outside source, run tests/types/demo, save rag.json and submit one original predicted regression plus an explained policy tradeoff.

Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Install three local packages, save actual lifecycle/answer experiments and add an original regression.

hints: Find the exact input, scope or metric rule the case evaluates.
Keep vector similarity, access and answer quality separate.
Install three local packages, save actual lifecycle/answer experiments and add an original regression.
exercises.solution: Finite exact quoting/provenance is different from broad answer quality and trustworthy sources.

lessons.title: Tools propose, application code decides
lessons.summary: Schemas, permissions & idempotent actions
objectives: Bind tool execution to authenticated identity.
Validate domain invariants after parsing.
Prevent duplicate effects across retries.

exercises.title: The model supplies an administrator role
exercises.prompt: A tool argument includes `role: admin`. What should establish the authorization context?

hints: A tool argument is data from an untrusted producer.
Identity comes from the application session.
Evaluate permissions outside model output.
exercises.solution: Use authenticated identity and server-side policy. Do not accept role or tenant arguments as authorization proof. Reject unnecessary fields in strict schemas and verify ownership inside the service.

exercises.title: A successful tool result is lost
exercises.prompt: An expense is committed but the orchestrator times out. What prevents duplication on retry?
options: Ask the model to remember it succeeded
Reuse a stable operation ID enforced by the expense service
hints: The orchestrator has an uncertain outcome.
Persistence must recognize the same intended action.
Apply idempotency at the business mutation boundary.
exercises.solution: Reuse a stable operation ID with transactional idempotency in the service. A prompt or model memory is not durable concurrency control. Reconcile ambiguous outcomes before creating a fresh operation.

lessons.title: Validate tool proposals without granting authority
lessons.summary: Treat tool names and arguments as strict untrusted data, then authorize separately.
objectives: Treat tool names and arguments as strict untrusted data, then authorize separately.
Implement strict proposal variants and argument shapes. Test unknown names, extra tenant/role fields, invented citation URLs and invalid integer usage before any side effect.
Explain validation versus permission. Verify malformed proposals stop dispatch and finish text cannot invent a completed action.

exercises.title: Tool check 1
exercises.prompt: A proposal contains valid JSON and an administrator role. What grants permission?
options: The role printed by the model
hints: Find the exact action, authority or observation boundary.
Keep proposals, approval, effects and returned evidence separate.
Treat tool names and arguments as strict untrusted data, then authorize separately.
exercises.solution: Valid syntax cannot grant a role. The application owns authenticated authority and action policy.

exercises.title: Tool check 2
exercises.prompt: A save_note proposal includes an extra tenant field. What should strict validation do?
hints: Find the exact action, authority or observation boundary.
Keep proposals, approval, effects and returned evidence separate.
Treat tool names and arguments as strict untrusted data, then authorize separately.
exercises.solution: The exact schema accepts only selected citation and label. Extra authority fields are rejected.

lessons.title: Approve one exact application-owned action
